title: Find the Monkey — A little lesson in thinking big
text:
Find the Monkey — A little lesson in thinking big
    
      
      
        
      
      
      
      
      
        ✳ A LITTLE LESSON IN THINKING BIG / 001
        Find themonkey.
        Stop buildingthe pedestal first.
        When a big idea has lots of moving parts, how do you know what to try first?
        ↓ FOLLOW THE STORY
      
      ONE BIG QUESTION / ONE SMALL EXPERIMENTSCROLL TO BEGIN ↓
    

    
      
        
          FIELD NOTES ✳ MAKE THE HARD PART VISIBLE
          
            
            
            ???
            THE MONKEY & THE PEDESTAL
          
          01 / THE BRIEFA VERY AMBITIOUS IDEA.
        
      

      
        
          
            01 / THE BRIEF
            A monkey.Three balls.One pedestal.
            Imagine someone gives you a wonderfully strange assignment: teach a monkey to juggle while standing on a tall pedestal.
            THE AMBITION ✳A juggling monkey, high above the ground.
            There are two big jobs: build the pedestal and find out whether the monkey can learn to juggle.
            Which one would you begin with?
            KEEP GOING ↓
          
        

        
          
            02 / THE CHOICE
            Where doyou begin?
            You have one week. Pick your first move.
            
              ABuild the pedestalClear plans. Quick progress. Something to show.↗
              BTry a tiny juggling lessonWill the monkey learn even one small step?↗
              CDesign the launch posterMake the big idea look irresistible.↗
            
            YOUR MOVEChoose an option to see what you would actually learn.
            ↻ Try another choice
          
        

        
          
            03 / THE TRAP
            A beautifulpedestal.Now what?
            Building the pedestal feels productive because you already know how. But a finished pedestal doesn't tell you whether the monkey can juggle.
            
              PEDESTAL WORKWhat you madePlans, paint, a polished platform.
              MONKEY WORKWhat you learnedWhether the risky part is even possible.
            
            Visible progress is not always meaningful progress.
          
        

        
          
            04 / THE IDEA
            Find themonkey.
            The monkey is not simply the hardest task. It's the important uncertainty that could make the rest of your work irrelevant.
            THE RULE ✳Find the assumption that matters most. Test it before polishing the easy parts.
            You may discover that the idea is possible. You may discover it needs to change. Either way, you've learned something useful.
          
        

        
          
            05 / A SMALLER AMBITION
            What abouta garden?
            Imagine planting a whole raised bed of vegetables. You're already picturing the harvest. Then the tiny sprouts start disappearing.
            Maybe slugs ate them. Maybe the conditions weren't right. Maybe the garden didn't get enough attention. You don't know yet.
            
              THE PEDESTAL?Buy more seeds. Add more boxes. Plan a bigger harvest.
              THE MONKEY?Can a small number of seedlings survive—and what is stopping them?
            
            A true story can start with a guess. A good experiment keeps the guess separate from the evidence.
          
        

        
          
            06 / YOUR NEXT MOVE
            The seedlingsvanished.
            What would teach you the most before planting the whole box again?
            
              APlant many more seedsSurely some will make it.↗
              BBuy every slug defenceAssume you've already found the culprit.↗
              CWatch six seedlings closelyCompare a few protected and unprotected plants; record what happens.↗
            
            YOUR MOVEChoose an approach. None guarantees a harvest.
            ↻ Try another approach
            A cover can also change temperature and moisture. Six plants won't give a definitive verdict—but observation beats an untested story.
          
        

        
          
            07 / THE PRACTICE
            Big ambition.Small experiment.
            This isn't an argument against building pedestals. Eventually, you'll need one. The trick is to avoid spending all your time there before the risky idea has been tested.
            FIND YOUR OWN MONKEY ↗
            TAKE THIS WITH YOUWhat would I need to learn first to know whether this idea is worth pursuing?
          
        
      
    

    
      
        08 / THE TINY EXPERIMENT LABNow it'syour turn.Pick a relatable example or bring your own ambition. No project plan required.
        
          
            START WITH A STORY
            A SMALL LIBRARY OF BIG IDEAS
            Choose an example…
            LOAD EXAMPLE ↗
            Or skip the examples and make this personal.
            
            The point is not to predict success. It's to learn enough to decide what to do next.
          
          
            01 WHAT MUST BE TRUE?
            
            02 WHAT IS ONE SMALL TEST?
            
            03 WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND?
            
            
              COPY MY EXPERIMENT ↗
              CLEAR
              
            
            Nothing you type here is sent to a server. Copy your notes to keep them.
          
        
      
    

    
      
        A FINAL THOUGHT
        Find the monkey.Then build the pedestal.
        Inspired by the monkey-and-pedestal idea associated with Astro Teller and X, the Moonshot Factory. This juggling story and its interactive examples are a playful adaptation.
        Being curious doesn't guarantee success. But a tiny test can save you from being confidently wrong for a very long time.

        
          🐒 Production note: No monkeys were trained
          during the making of this animation.
          The juggling balls are still negotiating their colours.
        
        ← BACK TO DERAILEDA CURIOUS DETOUR / NO FIXED DESTINATIONBACK TO TOP ↑

title: Who is leading the sardines? — Sardine Lab
text:
DERAILED / MARINE LIFE / AN AQUARIUM DETOUR




My aunt suspected there was a leader. The sardines declined to comment.



I visited Aquamarine Fukushima with my relatives and found myself completely mesmerized by the sardines in the big Kuroshio tank.
Hundreds of little silver fish, swimming together, turning together, somehow never bumping into one another. I could have watched them for hours.
Then a カラスエイ (pelagic stingray) glided through. The マイワシ (Japanese sardines) scattered, only to regroup and carry on as if nothing had happened.
My aunt had a theory:


“There must be a good leader.”


— My aunt, at the aquarium


I love this answer. It makes perfect sense from the outside. If a whole crowd moves in sync, surely someone must be calling the shots?
But… which fish? And how would everyone else get the memo in time?



Before making cartoon sardines swim around a browser, I wanted to know a little more about the two animals that started this whole detour.

  
    THE SCHOOL
    
    Sardinops melanostictus
    They gather near the sea surface, from coastal waters to offshore. Look closely: the row of dark spots along their sides has earned them the Japanese nickname 七つ星—“Seven Stars.” They also migrate north and south with the seasons.
    Why swim in a school? Possible advantages include safety in numbers, spotting danger sooner, and reproduction. There isn't just one explanation.
    Aquamarine's マイワシ profile ↗
  
  
    THE SURPRISE VISITOR
    
    Pteroplatytrygon violacea
    A dark-backed ray that swims through open ocean water rather than spending most of its life along the seabed. It moves with those broad, wing-like fins.
    Here's a fun twist: when feeding, it can actually turn belly-up and use its fins to help bring food toward its mouth. Our earlier upside-down sardine suddenly has some competition.
    Aquamarine's カラスエイ profile ↗
  

Aquamarine Fukushima’s Kuroshio tank recreates a little of the ocean’s eat-or-be-eaten world, bringing predators and prey together. Pelagic stingrays do eat sardines, but the one I watched wasn’t visibly hunting. It simply glided through, and the school parted around it, then flowed back together.
What fascinated me wasn’t the predator. It was how effortlessly hundreds of little fish responded together.



My aunt’s theory stayed with me. When hundreds of fish change direction together, it really does look as though someone must be giving instructions.
But what if nobody is?
I couldn’t bring the aquarium home, so I made a small version in my browser. First I drew one sardine. I gave it a direction, a speed, and a tail that moved. Then I made 47 more.
Forty-eight swimming fish are not automatically a school. Without paying attention to one another, they’re simply 48 individuals sharing a tank.
That gave me a better question: what does each fish need to notice about its neighbours for a school to appear?



Here’s the tank I built. Nobody has been appointed leader. Each fish has its own position and direction; the Schooling switch lets it respond to nearby fish.
Try switching between Independent and Schooling. Don’t change anything else at first. Do you notice a difference in how the group moves?
The three sliders below—separation, alignment, and cohesion—are the ingredients. You can play with them now, or meet them one at a time just below the tank.

  
    
      THE SARDINE LAB / AN EXPERIMENT
      
    
    No leader. Just neighbours.
  

  
    
    
      48 SARDINES
      48 FISH · AVG 0 PX/S
    
  

  
    
      
        01 / FISH GENERATOR
        Same species. Slightly different individuals.
      
      
        Number of fish 48
          
        
        Fish size 38%
          
        
        Body length 120
          
        
        Body depth 32
          
        
      
      
        ↝ New proportions
        ↻ New school
      
    

    
      
        02 / MOVEMENT ENGINE
        Each fish has its own heading and speed.
      
      
        Free swim
        Follow target
      
      Fish choose their own paths.
      
        Swim speed 1.1
          
        
        Turning agility 2.5
          
        
      
      
        ✳ New destination
        
          
          Trace one fish (not the leader)
        
      
    

    
      
        03 / SCHOOLING RULES
        What if each fish notices its neighbours?
      
      
        Independent
        Schooling
      
      Each fish notices only nearby neighbours.
      
        Three local rules
        
          Separation 1.4
            
          
          Alignment 1.0
            
          
          Cohesion 1.0
            
          
        
      
    
  

  
    Pause swimming
    Reset experiment
  
  Start by comparing Independent and Schooling. Then experiment with the separation, alignment, and cohesion sliders. The dotted amber path traces one fish—not a leader. For a leader-free experiment, stay in Free swim; tapping the tank gives every fish a shared destination.




I found it easier to understand the model by thinking about three ordinary problems. None requires a clever fish in charge. Each only requires a fish to pay attention to its neighbours.


Imagine walking through a crowded station. Someone steps into your personal space, and you move aside.
Separation is the fish version of that. In my model, a sardine turns away from neighbours that get too close. It doesn’t need to know where the whole school is headed; it only needs to avoid crowding the fish beside it.
Try it: With Schooling selected, slide Separation down to zero, then bring it back up. Look for changes in how closely the fish bunch together.



Now imagine walking with a group of friends. They’re all beginning to turn left, so you turn a little left too.
Alignment helps neighbouring fish face similar directions. Each fish considers the headings of fish nearby and adjusts its own. Nobody sends out a message saying, “Everyone turn now.”
Try it: Turn Alignment down to zero, then increase it again. Watch whether nearby fish tend to point the same way.



If you get distracted while walking with friends, eventually you notice they’re farther away. You head back toward them.
Cohesion does something similar. Each simulated fish steers toward the average position of its nearby neighbours. It isn’t chasing a designated leader—just trying not to lose the group.
Try it: Reduce Cohesion to zero, then restore it. Does the group seem more scattered or more connected?
These rules work together, so changing one slider won’t always produce an instant, tidy result. The tank is a place to observe, not a machine that guarantees the same pattern every time.




This experiment is inspired by Boids, a model introduced by computer graphics researcher Craig Reynolds in 1987. The three rules are simple: give your neighbours room, pay attention to their direction, and stay near the group.
Here’s the lovely part. No individual fish has to know what the whole school looks like. Each reacts to nearby fish, yet a larger, coordinated-looking pattern can appear.
That has a name: emergence—a group-level pattern arising from many local interactions.
Does that prove my aunt was wrong about the real sardines? No. A two-dimensional browser model isn’t a real aquarium. Real fish use their senses, navigate three-dimensional water, and respond to far more than three rules.
But it shows something important: a leader isn’t necessary to produce movement that looks coordinated.



Now I’m back at the moment that started this detour: the カラスエイ gliding through the マイワシ, and the school opening around it.
My simulated tank doesn’t have a stingray. Not yet.
Would a moving obstacle be enough to make a similar gap appear? Would the fish react directly to the ray, to their neighbours’ reactions, or both? I can’t answer that from what I saw through the glass—and this first experiment can’t either.
Which gives me another question to investigate. One aquarium visit, one comment from my aunt, and somehow I’ve ended up teaching 48 imaginary sardines to be good neighbours.

“There must be a good leader.”Maybe. Or maybe the fish just need good neighbours.


The real animals: マイワシ, カラスエイ, and Aquamarine Fukushima’s Kuroshio tank. The model: inspired by Craig Reynolds’ 1987 Boids work; a two-dimensional illustration, not a reconstruction of the aquarium encounter. DERAILED #16 · Gomasu #115.

title: How did Vancouver move one hour away from Seattle?
text:
DERAILED / CLOCKS & COORDINATES / NOVEMBER 2026




Nothing moved on the map. But on November 1, 2026, the clocks on either side of the border stopped agreeing.

The two cities are as close as they were yesterday. British Columbia decided to keep most of its clocks on UTC−7, while Washington State still turns back to UTC−8 for winter. The result? Vancouver and Seattle no longer share the same winter time.


A clock is a surprisingly political object. Start with Vancouver and Seattle; switch the date and watch what changes.

 INTERACTIVE EXPLORATION 


  
    01The border
    02The West
    03Across Canada
  
  Two neighbouring cities. One hour of difference.
  
    
      CHOOSE A DATE
      
        Oct 31, 2026
        Nov 2, 2026
      
    
    
      VANCOUVER COMPARED WITH
      Seattle
    
  
  
    
      BRITISH COLUMBIA
      
      9:00 AM
      UTC−7
    
    =
    
      WASHINGTON
      
      9:00 AM
      UTC−7
    
  
  Loading clock comparison…
  
    
    Loading geographic data…
     Selected cities  Great-circle distance
  
  
    The physical distance doesn't change.
    GeoNames representative points. Turf.js computes great-circle distance; the line is illustrative, not a driving route or time-zone boundary.
  
  


Try it: Start with Seattle and flip the date. Then select The West, add San Francisco or Calgary, and finally select Across Canada to discover Newfoundland’s half-hour offset.




On October 31, Vancouver, Seattle and San Francisco are all at UTC−7. On November 2, Washington and California have fallen back to UTC−8 while Vancouver stays on UTC−7.
At 9:00 AM in Vancouver, the clock in Seattle reads 8:00 AM. The difference will disappear again when the U.S. starts daylight saving time in March 2027, assuming the rules stay the same.
And the travel distance? Exactly unchanged. The Washington State Department of Transportation notes that an approximately four-hour Amtrak journey can appear as three hours in one direction and five in the other when shown in local departure and arrival times.
Explore the Western cities ↑



Before 2026, Vancouver and Victoria moved their clocks twice a year. Fort St. John already stayed at UTC−7 all year. Southeastern BC communities historically followed Mountain Time arrangements.
Calgary is another twist: Alberta is also staying on UTC−6 year-round from November 2026. That keeps Calgary one hour ahead of Vancouver while Seattle moves one hour behind.
One provincial boundary never guaranteed one clock rule. And a place’s IANA time-zone ID does not, by itself, explain which local government made that rule.
Compare BC and Alberta ↑



Toronto still falls back, so its winter difference from Vancouver shrinks from three hours to two. And St. John’s, Newfoundland, follows a half-hour time zone: its winter UTC offset is −3:30 rather than a whole number of hours.
The map expands, but the governing idea remains small: a geographic distance is not a time difference.
Explore across Canada ↑



A point. GeoNames provides representative city coordinates and identifiers.
A name. GeoNames also supplies IANA identifiers such as America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton, and America/St_Johns. They encode time-zone histories, not a single permanent offset.
A rule on a date. Government decisions determine local time policies. The R + DuckDB preparation script joins the GeoNames places to explicitly documented UTC offsets for two instants and exports a small JSON file. JavaScript reads that file to update the clocks; Turf.js computes the distances.
This is deliberately a dated editorial snapshot, not a universal time-zone conversion service. The source definitions and the rules are kept separate.



The next time someone says two cities are “in the same time zone,” there’s a useful follow-up question:
On which date?


Sources & method. Place coordinates: GeoNames (CC BY 4.0). Clock policies: Government of BC, Government of Alberta, Washington State, NIST, and St. John’s 2026 clock-change history. Amtrak travel example: WSDOT. The comparison uses 16:00 UTC on October 31 and November 2, not live clocks. Selected city points are not time-zone polygons. Editorial issue · Research issue.

And the travel distance? Exactly unchanged. The Washington State Department of Transportation notes that an approximately four-hour Amtrak journey can appear as three hours in one direction and five in the other when shown in local departure and arrival times.

title: How did Vancouver move one hour away from Seattle?
text:
Before 2026, Vancouver and Victoria moved their clocks twice a year. Fort St. John already stayed at UTC−7 all year. Southeastern BC communities historically followed Mountain Time arrangements.
Calgary is another twist: Alberta is also staying on UTC−6 year-round from November 2026. That keeps Calgary one hour ahead of Vancouver while Seattle moves one hour behind.
One provincial boundary never guaranteed one clock rule. And a place’s IANA time-zone ID does not, by itself, explain which local government made that rule.

title: How did Vancouver move one hour away from Seattle?
text:
Toronto still falls back, so its winter difference from Vancouver shrinks from three hours to two. And St. John’s, Newfoundland, follows a half-hour time zone: its winter UTC offset is −3:30 rather than a whole number of hours.
The map expands, but the governing idea remains small: a geographic distance is not a time difference.

A point. GeoNames provides representative city coordinates and identifiers.
A name. GeoNames also supplies IANA identifiers such as America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton, and America/St_Johns. They encode time-zone histories, not a single permanent offset.
A rule on a date. Government decisions determine local time policies. The R + DuckDB preparation script joins the GeoNames places to explicitly documented UTC offsets for two instants and exports a small JSON file. JavaScript reads that file to update the clocks; Turf.js computes the distances.
This is deliberately a dated editorial snapshot, not a universal time-zone conversion service. The source definitions and the rules are kept separate.
